relations.subject: index:index-span
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - the span IS the representation a pushed-down predicate takes; the page defines one in terms of the other
relations.evidence: The query predicates are translated into spans in the query plan and passed to the Indexer. Spans simply express the predicates in terms of data ranges.

relations.subject: service:query-service
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused
relations.evidence: During query execution, the query planner selects the most appropriate index path based on the query predicates (filters). Once the index path is chosen, the query engine requests the Index Service to perform a scan.

relations.subject: service:query-service
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused
relations.evidence: During execution, depending on the query, using applicable indexes, the Query node works with the Index and Data nodes to retrieve and perform the planned operations. Because Couchbase is a modular clustered database, you scale out data, index, and query services to fit your performance and availability goals.

relations.subject: service:query-service
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - the phase model (Scan-Fetch-Join-Sort-Project) is an execution model, and the page states that phases are conditional and repeatable
relations.evidence: The following figure shows all the possible phases a SELECT query goes through to return the results. Not all queries need to go through every phase, some go through many of these phases multiple times. For example, the Query Service skips the Sort phase when it does not include an ORDER BY clause; and the Scan-Fetch-Join phases execute multiple times for correlated subqueries.

relations.subject: index:index-span

relations.subject: index:index-span
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - a missing Low does not mean 'no lower bound' by symmetry with High: it means the scan starts at MISSING, which is a specific value in SQL++'s type order and the reason the covering-index MISSING rule exists
relations.evidence: A "Low" field in the range indicates the start value. If "Low" is missing, the scan starts with `MISSING`.

relations.subject: index:index-span
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - the deduplication rule is a property of span construction itself, and the asymmetry (duplicates go, overlaps stay) is the kind of thing that surprises readers of a plan
relations.evidence: In this example, the predicate `id = 10 OR id = 20` produces two independent ranges and both of them are pushed to index scan. Duplicate ranges are eliminated, but overlaps are not eliminated.

relations.subject: n1ql:in-operator
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused
relations.evidence: In this example, the predicate is `id IN [10,20]` (that is, id = 10 OR id = 20). After eliminating the duplicates, each element is pushed as a separate range to index scan.

relations.subject: n1ql:in-operator
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - above 8192 elements the Index service stops using ranges and scans the whole key; that is a forced substitution of mechanism, which is what this predicate records
relations.evidence: In version 4.5, up to 8192 IN elements are pushed as separate ranges to the index service. If the number of elements exceed 8192, then the index service performs a full scan on that key.

relations.subject: n1ql:in-operator
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - recorded because the page states a version, but see cross_product_finding: the sentence is really dating the 8192 limit, and it is a Server version on a Capella page, so phase 2 should treat this as evidence about the DOCS, not a supported claim about Capella
relations.evidence: In version 4.5, up to 8192 IN elements are pushed as separate ranges to the index service. If the number of elements exceed 8192, then the index service performs a full scan on that key.

relations.subject: n1ql:like-operator
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - a trailing-wildcard LIKE is rewritten into an equivalent two-sided range, which is why it can be pushed at all
relations.evidence: In this example, the predicate `name LIKE "American%"` is transformed to `name >= "American"` AND `name < "Americao"` (where "Americao" is the next string in SQL++ collation order after "American") and then pushed to index scan. In the LIKE predicate, the % means match with any number of any characters.

relations.subject: n1ql:like-operator
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - the closest promoted predicate for 'this rewrite is only correct because of the collation order'. Not a service dependency in the deployment sense; phase 2 may want a `dependsOnSemantics` predicate, and I have flagged that rather than minting one on thin evidence.
relations.evidence: In this LIKE predicate '%' is the leading portion of the string, so we can't push any portion of the string to the index service. `""` is the lowest string. `[]` is an empty array and is greater than every string value in the SQL++ collation order.

notable_absence.finding: This is the only page of the five with NO Related Links section at all - it ends at a three-sentence Summary - and yet it is the page the other four all link INTO, three of them at the same anchor (`index-scans.md#query-execution-details`). So the hub of this cluster is a dead end: a reader routed here from covering-indexes.md, index_pushdowns.md, early-filters-and-pagination.md or groupby-aggregate-performance.md has no documented way back or onward, and the page's own body links out only twice, both to prerequisites (Import Sample Data, Query Context). It also never links index_pushdowns.md, although index_pushdowns.md's Predicate Pushdown section explicitly delegates its detail here ('Refer to section [Index Scans](index-scans.md) for more information') - the delegation is one-way. Second absence: the page names the plan operator `IndexScan3` in a code block and in one sentence, and never explains the 3, never lists the other scan operators (IntersectScan, OrderedIntersectScan, UnionScan, DistinctScan, IndexCountScan3) that the sibling pages treat as decisive, and never says which of the thirty examples would produce which operator. The scan-operator vocabulary is used as though defined and is defined nowhere in the corpus.

cross_component_finding: The page contains a complete predicate-to-span translation semantics - thirty worked examples, plus a four-step algorithm for combining AND predicates ('Combined Low becomes highest of both Low values (NULL is the lowest.)' ... 'Repeat Steps 1 to 3 for each AND clause.') - and none of it is modellable as triples without inventing a per-predicate-shape vocabulary of about thirty terms. I have extracted the rules that generalise (inclusion enum, missing High/Low defaults, redundancy elimination, EMPTY SPAN, duplicate-not-overlap elimination, the IN limit, the LIKE rewrite and its leading-wildcard failure, the functional-index failure, parameter transparency) and deliberately not extracted the individual examples, which are instances rather than facts. Phase 2 should know that this page's real content is an algorithm, and that the ontology can hold its inputs and outputs but not the algorithm itself - which is a limit of the modelling approach, not a defect of the page. One inconsistency worth recording: the inclusion enum table gives NULL as the Low value for `id <= 10` and for the EMPTY SPAN case, while the prose says a missing Low means the scan starts with MISSING. NULL and MISSING are different values in SQL++ - groupby-aggregate-performance.md states outright that 'NULLS and MISSING are two separate groups' - so the tables and the prose on this page use NULL to mean two different things, and a reader cannot tell whether the span really starts at NULL or at MISSING.
cross_product_finding: 'In version 4.5, up to 8192 IN elements are pushed as separate ranges to the index service' is a Couchbase Server release reference on a Capella page that has no versions, sitting in a NOTE callout in the middle of Example 11. It is the only version number on any of the five pages in this batch. Capella is continuously deployed, so 'In version 4.5' cannot be read by a Capella user at all: either the limit applies (and the clause is noise) or it has changed since (and the number is stale). The id version:server-4-5 already exists in the corpus for exactly one reason - the Server copy of this same page - which is the tell that this sentence was never rewritten for Capella. Phase 2 should treat the availableSince relation I recorded from it as a docs defect marker rather than a product fact. The rest of the page has been Capella-ised properly (travel-sample 'supplied with Couchbase Capella', pre-installed def_inventory_* indexes, query context on the inventory scope), which makes the one survivor more conspicuous, not less.
